To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) private providers are heterogeneous in terms of the quality of care that they provide; (2) entry rates and the quality of care are positively correlated with local income; and ( 3) the quality of care is below recommended (but unregulated) levels, especially in low- income districts.
(1) private suppliers of child care respond to the demand for quality and (2) the demand for quality is heterogeneous across space.

1) the entry rate and the quality of private child care centers are higher in high-income neighborhoods; 2) the entry rate is positively related to local household income, while the quality of provision is negatively related to local household incomes, which suggests the existence of an inverse relationship between the entry rate and quality of provision across neighborhoods; and 3) the quality of child care provision is highly heterogeneous across neighborhoods and centers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the economic behavior of private suppliers of child care and its determinants.
the role of local income in shaping the supply of private child care and the heterogeneity in the provision of child care services in Sao Paulo.
the determinants of the supply side of the child care market.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we document the existence of a market for child care in Sao Paulo, where the quality of provision is heterogeneous and responds to local household income.
the child care market in Brazil is highly heterogeneous across districts and the quality of provision is systematically higher in richer districts.

the quality of provision is higher in richer districts and that a considerable number of child care centers do not meet the recommended (but not legally mandated) quality standards, which is especially true in poorer districts.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the market approach is unlikely to deliver uniform quality across households, and that regulations may be needed to achieve more equitable provision.
the market approach to expanding the supply of care can lead to substantial heterogeneity in the provision of care, which can be addressed by a combination of subsidies and regulations.
the market approach is likely to be more effective when combined with policies that increase the demand for high quality care.
